clue.text: Capers used by brewers?

explanation.surface: A question about what brewers make use of.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are skips or leaps, as are hops; the dried flowers of the hop plant flavour beer, so brewers use them.

clue.text: Mickey's home in Cornwall

explanation.surface: Where a famous cartoon rodent lives, apparently in the far south-west of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Mickey is Mickey Mouse. Mousehole is a fishing village in Cornwall, England's south-westernmost county.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartoon mouse would live in a small hole in the skirting board; the same name belongs to a Cornish fishing village.

clue.text: Low sound of Greek night-hooter?

parts.note: an owl is the bird that hoots at night

explanation.surface: Asks what noise a nocturnal bird from Greece might make.
explanation.definitionFit: A growl is a deep, rumbling noise made in the throat, as by an angry dog.

clue.text: Lines in old books with copy in excess of space available

definitions.text: copy in excess of space available

indicators.note: the lines are placed inside the abbreviation for the old books

parts.note: OT, the Old Testament, is the older set of books of the Bible
verse is writing set out in lines

explanation.surface: Sounds like a description of printing practice in antique volumes.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing, overset matter is type set beyond what the page or column has room for.

clue.text: First-class coins, perhaps, for overseas capital

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters given might be arranged some other way

parts.note: A1 means first-class, with the figure 1 read as the letter I
taken as written

explanation.surface: Top-quality money being spent in a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of A1 (read as AI) plus COINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicosia is the capital city of Cyprus, a country abroad from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: An additional bonus

explanation.surface: A phrase describing an extra perk.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means extra or added; as a noun it means an advantage or welcome extra.

clue.text: Ignited high explosive which is pliant

parts.note: something ignited has been lit

explanation.surface: A lit bomb that is somehow flexible.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe describes a body that bends easily and gracefully, supple like something pliant.

clue.text: Plans for television's first megastars to be worked out

indicators.note: letters to be worked out are to be rearranged until they make sense
first asks for only the opening letter of the word television

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A TV channel's schemes for its biggest names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' gives T from 'television's'; 'to be worked out' shuffles T with MEGASTARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stratagems are schemes or cunning plans devised to gain an advantage.

clue.text: No room underneath the arches for Bobby?

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a policeman has nowhere to stay under a railway viaduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under the arches' suggests rough sleeping beneath railway arches, but these are the arches of the feet. A bobby is a British police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A foot with fallen arches leaves no gap beneath; the same word is slang for a plodding police officer.

clue.text: Wealthy underworld boss?

explanation.surface: A rich crime lord.
explanation.walkthrough: Pluto, Roman ruler of the dead, was linked with riches from below the earth; his Greek name gives 'plutocrat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of the dead was also seen as a giver of riches, ruler of the land below the earth.

clue.text: Seat Carol ordered for the non-stop flight

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone books a direct plane seat for a woman called Carol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests air travel, but it is a flight of stairs; 'ordered' signals an anagram of SEAT CAROL.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving staircase is a set of steps that keeps running continuously.

clue.text: Crossbow exponents who sit?

parts.note: read the crossbow as a bow drawn across strings by seated musicians, not an archer's weapon

explanation.surface: Seated archers skilled with a medieval weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Players of the large stringed instrument sit and draw a bow across its strings.

clue.text: Lifting the foot that is shortened

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word foot is cut down to its usual abbreviation

parts.note: the unit of length, a foot

explanation.surface: Raising a foot that has been reduced in length.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting' looks like raising, but is slang for stealing; 'shortened' turns FOOT into FT.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something is slang for stealing it, so lifting is stealing.

clue.text: Amphetamine check of seventy on the road

parts.note: speed is street slang for amphetamine
a limit is a check or restraint

explanation.surface: A drug test for a driver doing seventy.
explanation.walkthrough: Seventy miles per hour is the top permitted speed on British motorways and dual carriageways.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventy mph is the maximum legal rate of travel on major British roads.

clue.text: Sibyl's benefit announced

indicators.note: announced means the word for a benefit is spoken, and we write what it sounds like

parts.note: a profit is a gain or benefit

explanation.surface: A woman named Sibyl's gain is made public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sibyl's' is read as 'Sibyl is': a sibyl was a prophetess of the ancient world.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibyl was a woman of classical times who foretold the future, a seer.

clue.text: Highest country in which to find Ness, say?

parts.note: head as an adjective means chief or highest
land means a country

explanation.surface: Asks for the loftiest nation in which to find the Loch Ness monster.
explanation.walkthrough: Ness suggests Loch Ness, but a ness is a promontory, as in Scottish place names.
explanation.definitionFit: A ness is a cape or promontory jutting into the sea.

clue.text: Loving a party, telephone!

parts.note: a do is a party
to ring is to telephone

explanation.surface: An excited instruction to phone about a party one loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoring means feeling deep love and devotion.

clue.text: Evens out colour in durable earthenware

parts.note: irons smooths out creases, evening out cloth
a tone is a shade of colour

explanation.surface: Smoothing out the shade of hard-wearing pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironstone china is a hard, heavy white pottery.

clue.text: It is put into orbit for a brighter outlook

definitions.text: It is put into orbit for a brighter outlook

parts.words: It is put into orbit for a brighter outlook
parts.note: orbit here is the eye socket; a small cup of lotion is held against it to refresh the sight

explanation.surface: Something launched into space to improve the forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: A small cup shaped to fit the eye, used to rinse it with lotion.

clue.text: Dashes in rum-punch and whisky-sour?

parts.note: dashes are not splashes of mixer but the short joining strokes printed inside these compound words

explanation.surface: A cocktail-maker adding splashes of flavouring to drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The short strokes joining words such as rum-punch are linking punctuation marks.

clue.text: Caterpillar saw spineless person

parts.note: to saw is to cut
a worm is a weak, contemptible person

explanation.surface: A caterpillar spotted a coward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' looks like the past of 'see' but is the verb to cut with a saw.
explanation.definitionFit: Moth larvae that sever young plants at ground level are a kind of caterpillar.

clue.text: More brutish-sounding greyhound, perhaps

indicators.note: sounding means the word for more brutish is said, and we write what it sounds like

parts.note: coarser means ruder and more brutish

explanation.surface: A dog that seems rougher than the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog used in coursing, chasing hares by sight, such as a greyhound, is an example.

clue.text: Mark of Lincoln in the fifties?

indicators.note: Lincoln's name is placed inside the letters for fifties

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so two fifties give LL
Abe is Abraham Lincoln's familiar first name

explanation.surface: A trademark of Lincoln's from the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fifties' suggests the decade, but it gives two Roman fifties.
explanation.definitionFit: A label is a tag or mark identifying something.

clue.text: Continue to attack bowling with slender stick

parts.note: in cricket the batter attacks the bowling, so to bat is to attack it
to go on is to continue, so on gives that sense

explanation.surface: A cricket batter keeps hitting the ball with a thin stick.
explanation.walkthrough: To bat on is to keep batting; in cricket the bowler delivers the ball and the batter strikes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a thin rod, as used by a conductor or relay runner.

clue.text: The most fleshy fruit-bug

parts.note: a plum is a fruit
a pest is a bug or insect nuisance

explanation.surface: An insect that eats the juiciest fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumpest means roundest and fullest-bodied, carrying most flesh.

clue.text: Silver-lined pot of heathen?

indicators.note: the pot has silver as its lining, placed inside it

parts.note: a pan is a cooking pot
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A silver-coated vessel belonging to an unbeliever.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagan follows a non-Christian, often polytheistic, religion.

clue.text: County no longer known

explanation.surface: An English shire that has faded from memory.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England; 'kent' is an old Scots past form of ken, to know.
explanation.definitionFit: A south-eastern English shire, and an archaic form meaning recognised or familiar.

clue.text: Christian followers in revolt, in the main?

definitions.text: Christian followers in revolt, in the main?

parts.words: Christian followers in revolt, in the main?
parts.note: Christian is Fletcher Christian, who led the Bounty uprising at sea; the main is the ocean

explanation.surface: Churchgoers who are mostly rebellious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' looks like 'mostly' but means at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors who rose against their captain on the Bounty followed Fletcher Christian.

clue.text: Theatre-in-the-round?

parts.note: a famous round London playhouse, and also a spherical thing

explanation.surface: A stage with the audience all around it.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's playhouse in Southwark was circular, and a sphere is round.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's circular Southwark playhouse bears the name of a sphere.

clue.text: Sort of square bottom makes one lean, thus

parts.note: a T-square is a draughtsman's ruler, so T is a sort of square
the end is the bottom of something

explanation.surface: A drawing tool whose base makes it tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: To tend is to incline or lean towards something.

clue.text: Harsh, stern giant reformed!

indicators.note: reformed means the letters are formed again in a new order

explanation.surface: A severe giant has mended his ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent means severe and sharply critical.
